meta.title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) — disease data
meta.disclaimer: Educational reference compiled from published medical sources. Not a diagnosis, treatment plan, or substitute for a clinician. CRPS is diagnosed clinically; there is no gold-standard laboratory test.

identity.name: Complex regional pain syndrome

icd10_gm_germany.type_1: G90.5 (CRPS Typ I / sympathische Reflexdystrophie / Morbus Sudeck)
icd10_gm_germany.note: Exact 5-character ICD-10-GM codes vary by limb and laterality; coding practice should follow current DIMDI/BfArM tables.

identity.orphanet: ORPHA:83450 (rare / orphan disease designation in EU and US)
former_names: Reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD) — now CRPS type I
identity.definition: A rare chronic pain condition, usually in a distal limb after trauma or surgery, with continuing regional pain that is disproportionate in intensity or duration to the expected course of the injury, plus sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema, and motor/trophic abnormalities. Pain is regional and does not follow a single nerve or dermatome.

classification.iasp_pain_class: Chronic primary pain; IASP has also proposed that many patients meet nociplastic pain descriptors

subtypes.name: CRPS type I
subtypes.note: No identifiable major peripheral nerve lesion. Far more common than type II. Clinical features are otherwise the same as type II.

subtypes.name: CRPS type II
subtypes.note: Documented peripheral nerve injury is present. Distinguished from ordinary neuropathic pain by obligatory autonomic signs and spread beyond the injured nerve territory.

subtypes.name: CRPS in partial remission
subtypes.note: Valencia 2021 subtype: previously met full Budapest criteria but no longer does, while residual signs/symptoms remain. Pain may still be disabling.

subtypes.name: CRPS-NOS (not otherwise specified)
subtypes.note: Some CRPS-like features without ever meeting full Budapest criteria, and no better alternative diagnosis.

phenotypes_informal.name: Warm CRPS
phenotypes_informal.features: Increased temperature, redness, vasodilation; more typical of early/inflammatory presentations

phenotypes_informal.name: Cold CRPS
phenotypes_informal.features: Cooler limb, pallor/cyanosis, vasoconstriction; associated with more chronic courses in some series

classification.note_on_staging: Bonica's historic 3-stage model (acute / dystrophic / atrophic) is not supported as a reliable timeline. Symptom clusters do not map cleanly onto duration.

rarity.us_5yr_incidence_estimate: About 0.07% over 5 years in one US database analysis (ICD-9 based; may be inflated).

incidence_per_100000_person_years.study: Sandroni et al. 2003 — Olmsted County, Minnesota
incidence_per_100000_person_years.notes: Population-based; older IASP criteria; female:male ≈ 4:1; median onset age 46.
Population-based; older IASP criteria; female:male ≈ 3:1; peak age 61–70.

prevalence_examples.study: South Korea electronic health data (Bang / Kim series; ICD-9 era)
prevalence_examples.value: About 26 per 100,000 (prevalence estimate; coding may inflate).

epidemiology.sex: Women are affected about 3–4 times more often than men.
epidemiology.age: Incidence rises with age; highest between about 50 and 80 years. Also occurs in children (outside most adult reviews).
epidemiology.limb: Upper limb (hand/arm) more often than lower limb in several Western series; some East Asian coding studies report more lower-limb involvement.

inciting_events.most_common: Fracture (about 44–46% of cases in classic population studies)
other: Surgery (fracture fixation, carpal tunnel release ~2–5%, foot/ankle surgery ~4%, Dupuytren surgery 4.5–40% in older series)
Cast/splint immobilisation (systematic-review signal for increased risk)
Minor procedures (e.g. IV cannulation) in some reports
Rare spontaneous onset without identified trauma

post_injury_rates.reported_range: about 2–25% depending on criteria and follow-up
up to ~13% in some older series; near 0% when Budapest criteria applied strictly in one 100-patient study

risk_factors.factor: High pain intensity in the first week after injury (e.g. NRS 7–8/10 after wrist fracture)
Open fracture / crush injury vs simple fracture
Pre-existing chronic pain (RA, migraine, widespread pain)

risk_factors.evidence: Associated with onset/persistence in unadjusted prospective analyses; not a personality-type disease

pathophysiology.summary: Multifactorial. No single mechanism. Involves neurogenic inflammation, immune/autoimmune signals, peripheral and central sensitisation, autonomic dysregulation, and cortical reorganisation. Psychological distress can amplify symptoms but CRPS is not a conversion or 'psychogenic' diagnosis.

mechanisms.name: Neurogenic / immune inflammation
mechanisms.detail: Elevated TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-2, IL-6; neuropeptides (CGRP, bradykinin, substance P) causing vasodilation and plasma extravasation. Acute CRPS skin shows up-regulated TNF-α and IL-6 vs the unaffected limb.

mechanisms.name: Autoimmune contribution
mechanisms.detail: Autoantibodies to β2-adrenergic, α1a-adrenergic, and muscarinic M2 receptors reported. Passive transfer of IgM/IgG can induce CRPS-like features in animal models. Some patients improve with IVIG in selected studies.

mechanisms.name: Peripheral sensitisation
mechanisms.detail: Inflammatory mediators lower nociceptor thresholds → hyperalgesia. Catecholamine sensitivity of peripheral fibres.

mechanisms.name: Central sensitisation and cortical change
mechanisms.detail: Dorsal-horn wind-up, NMDA involvement, allodynia. Reduced somatosensory cortical representation of the affected limb; body-perception disturbance (limb feels larger/foreign).

mechanisms.name: Autonomic / sympathetic coupling
mechanisms.detail: Upregulated adrenoreceptors on nociceptors; colour, temperature, and sweating asymmetry. Sympathetic blocks have not shown clear RCT benefit despite historical use.

mechanisms.name: Genetic / epigenetic
mechanisms.detail: Possible HLA and TNF-α associations. 2023 exome work suggested heritability in a subset (more in males) with SNPs in ANO10, P2RX7, PRKAG1, SLC12A9.

clinical_features.core: Continuing regional pain, usually distal limb, disproportionate to the injury, plus mixed sensory/autonomic/motor/trophic signs that fluctuate.
clinical_features.onset: Typically days to weeks after trauma; often within 8 weeks of a noxious event.
clinical_features.laterality: Usually unilateral. Bilateral onset should prompt alternative diagnoses.

categories.name: Sensory
symptoms_and_signs: Hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain to pinprick or other noxious stimuli)
Allodynia (pain from light touch, clothing, deep pressure, or joint movement)

categories.name: Vasomotor
symptoms_and_signs: Skin colour change or colour asymmetry (red, mottled, pale, cyanotic)
Temperature asymmetry (sign threshold often cited as >1 °C)

categories.name: Sudomotor / edema
symptoms_and_signs: Sweating changes or sweating asymmetry (hyperhidrosis or dryness)

categories.name: Motor / trophic
symptoms_and_signs: Trophic changes of skin, hair, or nails (glossy skin, hair growth change, brittle nails)

associated_burden: Anxiety, depression, pain-related fear / kinesiophobia (secondary, not causal personality)
Work disability: up to ~40% unable to return to work; about one-third of returners need job adaptation
Less common systemic associations reported: cognitive/word-finding issues, urologic urgency, GI dysmotility

diagnosis.method: Clinical diagnosis of exclusion using IASP Budapest criteria (2007/2010), with Valencia consensus assessment instructions (2021). Tests (thermography, 3-phase bone scan, QSART) may support or rule out mimics; they are not required.

budapest_clinical.compared_to: Original 1994 IASP criteria (similar sensitivity, lower specificity)

budapest_requirements: 1. Continuing pain that is disproportionate to any inciting event
2. Patient reports at least 1 symptom in 3 of 4 categories (sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema, motor/trophic)
3. Examiner finds at least 1 sign in 2 or more of those 4 categories at the visit
4. No other diagnosis better explains the signs and symptoms
valencia_clarifications_2021: Re-apply the full criteria at every assessment (signs fluctuate).
Spread = meeting full CRPS criteria in more than one limb.
Define 'asymmetry' and 'changes' carefully (see ICD-11 assessment notes).
Introduced CRPS in partial remission and retained CRPS-NOS.
differential_diagnosis: Post-traumatic or post-surgical neuropathic pain without CRPS features
Conversion disorder (must not be a default explanation)

management.guideline: UK Royal College of Physicians CRPS in adults (2nd edition) is widely cited as the high-quality integrated guideline. Four equal pillars: education, pain relief, physical rehabilitation, psychological intervention.
principles: Start rehabilitation early; delayed care is linked to worse function.
Individualise: evidence for most drugs/procedures in CRPS specifically is low or very low certainty.
Do not wait for a 'perfect' diagnosis before gentle, supervised movement if CRPS is suspected.
Strong opioids are generally avoided; refer to a pain specialist if considered.
Amputation is not a reliable cure; phantom/stump pain and recurrent CRPS are common.

pillars.name: Education
points: Explain nerve-function / inflammatory pain, not 'imagined' pain
Up to ~18 months, many people improve substantially (about 80% in one 2025 clinical review)
Involve family; teach pacing and flare-up plans
Distress and a 'strange-feeling' limb are common, not a sign of madness

pillars.name: Physical and occupational therapy
points: Desensitisation, gentle ROM, then graded loading
Graded motor imagery and mirror therapy (low-certainty benefit in Cochrane reviews)
Avoid forced painful mobilisation; also avoid complete disuse

pillars.name: Medicines (examples — clinician-directed)
points: Simple analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) first for residual trauma pain
Neuropathic agents: amitriptyline/nortriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin/pregabalin — modest effects extrapolated from neuropathic pain; CRPS-specific evidence is weak
Short steroid course sometimes used early (guidelines vary; evidence mixed)
Bisphosphonates (e.g. IV pamidronate) considered for early CRPS (<~4–6 months) — low-certainty; later-duration trials of other agents have failed
Ketamine infusions: possible short-term relief, not guideline-first-line; psychomimetic risks
Avoid starting strong opioids for CRPS in RCP guidance

pillars.name: Psychological intervention
points: CBT / pain-management programmes have moderate-certainty small benefits in chronic pain generally
Address anxiety, depression, sleep, compensation stress, fear of movement
CRPS is not caused by a specific personality type

interventional: Local-anaesthetic sympathetic blocks: historically common; RCTs suggest they are probably ineffective as pain treatment

Spinal cord stimulation or dorsal root ganglion stimulation: specialist option after failed integrated care; ACCURATE trial favoured DRG vs SCS in selected CRPS; complications and waning benefit occur
Do not use amputation as routine salvage
prevention_uncertain: Non-restrictive casting and early functional rehab after fracture
Vitamin C 500 mg/day for 50 days after wrist fracture: mixed meta-analyses; not a firm guideline mandate

prognosis.early_course: Acute CRPS often improves in the first 6 months.
prognosis.at_12_months: About 14–27% still fulfil Budapest criteria at 12 months in prospective series; in one CRPS I cohort with symptoms up to 6 months, 48% still met criteria 1 year later.
prognosis.at_18_months: NEJM 2025 clinical review: roughly 80% have substantial improvement by 18 months; later major improvement is less common.
prognosis.long_term: Between 1 and 8 years, average CRPS severity may change little. Residual mild pain, sensitivity, or swelling can persist even when people feel much better.
prognosis.work: Up to 40% do not return to work; ~1/3 of those who return need workplace adaptation.
prognosis.spread_risk: People who do not improve by ~18 months may develop spread or non-CRPS widespread/neuropathic pain.
